lesson.title: Ending the Spoils System: The Fight for a Merit Based Government
lesson.summary: After decades of federal jobs going to party loyalists rather than qualified workers, and after a president was shot by a disappointed office seeker, reformers finally forced Washington to hire and promote government employees based on merit.
lesson.body:
Since the era of Andrew Jackson, American presidents had rewarded political supporters with federal jobs under the frank principle that "to the victor belong the spoils." By the Gilded Age, this spoils system, discussed in the previous chapter alongside the broader corruption of Gilded Age politics, had hardened into a machine of institutionalized patronage: unqualified appointees filled government offices, officials spent their energy protecting their jobs rather than doing them, and officeholders were often expected to kick back part of their salaries to their party's campaign funds.

Pressure for reform built steadily through the 1870s and into the 1880s, led by reform minded Republicans nicknamed "Mugwumps," who broke with their party over its defense of patronage, along with civic organizations pushing for a professional civil service in which government jobs were awarded through competitive examination rather than political connections.

The event that turned reform from a minority cause into an unstoppable political demand came on July 2, 1881, when President James Garfield was shot at a Washington, D.C. train station by Charles Guiteau, a mentally disturbed man who had unsuccessfully sought a federal appointment and blamed his rejection on the political system. Garfield lingered for weeks before dying on September 19, 1881. Guiteau's own claim, offered at his trial, that his act was connected to the spoils system focused enormous public outrage directly onto the patronage practices that had shaped his grievance.

Garfield's death elevated Vice President Chester A. Arthur to the presidency. Arthur was a former Stalwart with deep ties to the New York patronage machine, and reformers expected little from him. To their surprise, feeling the full weight of public anger after the assassination, Arthur became a genuine advocate for civil service reform, setting the stage for the landmark law covered in the next chapter.
